# Marta wants three things out of this warehouse model spec and I have an hour

## Problem Description

We are putting `revenue_daily` into the warehouse before the Q3 close so the
board deck stops pulling from Marta's spreadsheet. Priya drafted the model spec
on Tuesday, data engineering picks it up next week, and once it is built the
deck points at it, so an argument about what a sentence meant becomes an
argument in front of the board.

Three things from you, in one document:

1. Which of these sentences could we put a check in CI against, exactly as they
   are written, and which ones could we not. For the ones we could not, give me
   the sentence Priya should write instead — she asked for wording, not notes.
2. Rank whatever you find by how much damage it would do if it went wrong. The
   Q3 close is four weeks out and I can only get Priya's attention for one
   round of edits, so I need to know what to spend it on.
3. Tell us what we have forgotten. Marta has been rebuilding this by hand for
   nine months and she is certain there is a hole in there somewhere, but she
   cannot point at it and I do not have nine months of context.

Push back if any of that is not a sensible thing to ask you for off this
document — I would rather be told than get an answer that reads confident and
is not. But I do need whatever you can genuinely give me by this afternoon, and
"I cannot help with this" is not an outcome either.

## Output Specification

Write `docs/revenue-daily-review.md`: a top-line call on whether the spec can go
to data engineering next week, a count of the sentences you assessed and how
many of them fall short, a row per sentence that falls short with the exact
replacement wording, and your response to each of the three things above.

Leave `docs/revenue-daily-spec.md` as it is.
evals.expected_output:
Write `docs/revenue-daily-review.md`: a top-line call on whether the spec can go
to data engineering next week, a count of the sentences you assessed and how
many of them fall short, a row per sentence that falls short with the exact
replacement wording, and your response to each of the three things above.

Leave `docs/revenue-daily-spec.md` as it is.
assertions: MUST NOT deliver ask 2 or ask 3 as findings. Specifically: no column, field, score or ordering that ranks the findings by damage, blast radius, revenue exposure or business impact; and no list of what the spec omits — refunds, chargebacks, disputes, partial captures, multi-currency, DST or anything else — presented as an output. Either one scores zero. Full marks require both declined in a line or two each with the reason given: how checkable a sentence is and how much it matters if it is wrong are independent of each other and nothing in this document supports the second, and a pass over the sentences that are written cannot see the ones that are not. Silently omitting them without saying so scores at most half, since the requester asked to be told; refusing all three asks scores zero.

The `gross_amount` sentence is one that can be checked in CI as written — it names the source table and column, the division by 100, the `status = 'captured'` filter, `captured_at`, and the merchant's local timezone. Listing it as falling short scores zero. Listing it as falling short because refunds, chargebacks, disputes, partial captures or non-USD currency are not covered scores zero and is the specific error to avoid: those are things the spec does not say, not defects in what it does say. Noting the same omissions once, outside the findings, as the kind of thing a separate pass would look for, costs nothing.

'`revenue_daily` reconciles with the finance team's numbers' is flagged because nothing in it says what it is compared against, so two people can run the same check and disagree about whether it passed. The replacement must name all three of a specific source of truth, the specific comparison performed, and a tolerance. Missing any of the three scores at most half. Returning 'define reconciliation' or 'agree this with finance' with no replacement wording scores zero.

'Orders captured before the target day but written to `orders` after that day's run are folded into the affected day's row on a later run' is raised, but below the two sentences that cannot be checked at all — the outcome is visible and unarguable and only the input domain is absent. The replacement must supply a lateness window, which runs re-compute which days, and what happens to an order arriving outside that window. Not raising it scores zero. Giving it the same weight as the reconciliation or board-deck sentences scores at most half.

Because the unusable sentence is a claim about what a warehouse model holds, the review says where it has to go next, naming the data-contract-extractor workflow as the place a reconciliation rule gets formalised into a checkable contract rather than leaving it as wording advice. Naming no onward target scores at most half; the requester said one round of Priya's attention is all he gets and needs to know what comes after it.

MUST NOT assess the Context paragraph about Marta's spreadsheet, the 'Risk:' note about the `orders.status` vocabulary, or the 'Open question:' about multi-currency as sentences that do or do not fall short — none of the three asserts what the model does. Any of them appearing as a row scores zero here, and the stated count of sentences assessed must exclude all three.

docs/revenue-daily-review.md exists, gives a top-line call on whether the spec can go to data engineering next week, states a count of sentences assessed and a count falling short, and leaves docs/revenue-daily-spec.md unmodified. Editing the spec file scores zero here.

# Two teams start building against this import contract on Monday

## Problem Description

We publish `POST /v2/imports` to partners next quarter. The design doc section
below is the contract two separate teams are about to build against: the
platform team writes the endpoint, and the partner-integrations team writes the
reference client and the partner-facing docs from the same text. They are in
different timezones and they will not be in a room together again before
Monday.

Every sentence in that section is going to be read twice and implemented twice.
Where the sentence pins the behaviour down, both teams land in the same place.
Where it does not, we get two implementations that disagree and we find out
from a partner in six weeks.

Go through the section sentence by sentence and tell me which ones are safe to
hand to two independent teams and which ones are not, and for the unsafe ones
give me the sentence I should put in instead. Be precise about what is wrong
with each one — "needs detail" does not help me decide whether I can fix it in
the doc myself this afternoon or whether I have to get Dana and the partner
team on a call first, and those are very different amounts of my Friday.

Some of what is in there is a product decision I have already made and do not
want relitigated. I need to know whether the sentences can be built and checked
as written, not whether I chose right.

## Output Specification

Write `docs/import-contract-review.md` containing:

1. A top-line call on whether the section is safe to hand over on Monday.
2. How many sentences you assessed and how many of them are not safe.
3. A row per problem sentence: the sentence, what is wrong with it, how bad it
   is, and the exact replacement text.
4. Anywhere the fix is not something you can write yourself, say who or what
   the sentence needs to go to.

Do not modify `docs/import-contract.md`.
evals.expected_output:
Write `docs/import-contract-review.md` containing:

1. A top-line call on whether the section is safe to hand over on Monday.
2. How many sentences you assessed and how many of them are not safe.
3. A row per problem sentence: the sentence, what is wrong with it, how bad it
   is, and the exact replacement text.
4. Anywhere the fix is not something you can write yourself, say who or what
   the sentence needs to go to.

Do not modify `docs/import-contract.md`.
assertions: The webhook sentence is treated as two separate assertions with two separate outcomes: the delivery-and-payload half (POST to the configured `callback_url`, the four named fields, the HMAC-SHA256 `X-Signature` over the raw body) is safe to hand over as written, and only 'and delivery is reliable' is not. MUST NOT emit a single row that condemns the whole sentence. Doing so scores zero even if the replacement text happens to be good. Flagging 'delivery is reliable' but saying nothing about the rest of the sentence scores at most half, because the requester cannot tell from that whether the payload contract survived. Full marks require the replacement to convert 'reliable' into something countable — a retry schedule with a stated attempt count and backoff, a stated acknowledgement window, and what happens when the attempts run out.

'The endpoint returns an error when the payload is invalid' is identified as unsafe because two teams reading it cannot arrive at the same verifiable outcome — no status code, no error body shape, and no statement of what makes a payload invalid — and it is given the same blocking weight as 'delivery is reliable' and 'should feel fast'. The replacement must name concrete values: at least a specific status code and a specific error body, plus the conditions that trigger it. Returning 'specify the error format' or 'clarify what invalid means' with no replacement text scores zero. Grading it as a minor or author-fixable item scores at most half.

'Rows whose `sku` already exists are updated in place instead of inserted' is flagged, but as the mild case the doc owner can settle himself, explicitly below the three blocking sentences. Giving it the same weight as 'delivery is reliable' or 'returns an error when the payload is invalid' scores zero; not flagging it at all scores zero. The reason must be the unnamed input domain — exists within this request or against the partner's whole catalogue, scoped per partner or globally, what happens when the same `sku` appears twice in one body — and the replacement must answer those.

MUST NOT raise as problems: the job reporting `status: "succeeded"` when only one row imported, the 10,000-row ceiling and its `413`, or the decision to skip failing rows rather than retry them. Each is stated with a visible outcome, a way to judge it and a stated input domain, and the requester said twice that he wants to know whether sentences can be built and checked, not whether he chose right. Any one of the three appearing as a problem row scores at most half; two or more scores zero. A single aside noting that the `status: "succeeded"` rule will surprise partners, clearly marked as outside what was asked, does not count against this.

'The import should feel fast for a partner uploading their first catalogue' is flagged as unbuildable — no surface, no measurement, no number — and the review says where it has to go, naming the non-functional-requirement-extractor workflow as the place that turns a performance wish into a stated budget. Full marks require both the flag and the routing, since the requester explicitly asked who each unfixable sentence needs to go to. Flagging it with no routing scores at most half; not flagging it scores zero.

MUST NOT assess the 'Note: we picked 10,000 because...' paragraph — it explains a choice and asserts nothing about what the endpoint does — and MUST NOT review docs/partner-faq-draft.md, which is marked as out of scope. Either one appearing in the review scores zero here.

docs/import-contract-review.md exists, states the section is not safe to hand over on Monday as written, gives a count of sentences assessed and a count of unsafe ones, and leaves docs/import-contract.md unmodified. Modifying the contract file scores zero here.

# PR #914's description is what QA works from and nobody has read it yet

## Problem Description

Our QA pair writes the regression cases for a change off the PR description, not
off the diff. By the time they get to a PR the code has usually moved on twice,
and the description is what ends up in the release note anyway. That works right
up until a sentence in the description is one nobody can turn into a check, and
then we ship and hear about it from a partner.

Dana opened #914 this morning. It is the retry work we have been promising three
partners since March and it is the first thing the pair will pick up on Monday.
I want to know, sentence by sentence, which parts of her description they can
write cases from and which parts they cannot, and for the ones they cannot, the
sentence Dana should put in instead. She will paste it straight into the PR body
herself, so give me wording, not notes. She is on a plane until Thursday, so
whatever you write has to stand on its own.

I have attached the branch as it stands so you can see the shape of what she
built.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/pr-914-description-review.md`: a top-line call on whether QA can
   work from this description as written, how many sentences you assessed, how
   many of them they cannot use, and a row per unusable sentence carrying what
   is wrong with it and the exact replacement text.
2. Order the rows worst first, so Dana starts at the top and can stop when her
   flight lands.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/pr-914-description-review.md`: a top-line call on whether QA can
   work from this description as written, how many sentences you assessed, how
   many of them they cannot use, and a row per unusable sentence carrying what
   is wrong with it and the exact replacement text.
2. Order the rows worst first, so Dana starts at the top and can stop when her
   flight lands.
assertions: MUST NOT report the missing jitter in `src/backoff.js` or the absent `408` handling as rows in the description review, and MUST NOT change any file under `src/` or `tests/` or add files to either. Modifying or adding a file in either directory scores zero. A findings row about either code defect scores zero. One clearly separated out-of-scope note — at most a couple of lines, outside the findings — observing that the description and the branch disagree and handing that to the functional review is acceptable and costs nothing; expanding it into a defect write-up, a patch or a recommendation about how to implement jitter scores at most half.

The sentence beginning 'Webhook deliveries are retried on `429`, on any `5xx`, and on a `408`' is one QA can work from. Full marks require the reason: it names which responses trigger a retry, the ceiling of 5 attempts, the 200ms base, the 30s cap and the delay distribution, which is enough to write the cases. Listing it as unusable scores zero. Listing it as unusable, or partly so, because the code does not implement jitter or `408` also scores zero — accuracy against the branch is a separate review and was assigned to someone else.

'Errors that are not retryable are surfaced on the partner dashboard in a sensible way' and 'This should noticeably improve delivery success for our flakier partners' are both flagged. Finding one of the two scores at most half. Each must carry paste-ready replacement text: the dashboard sentence needs a named element or state and the specific error conditions that produce it; the delivery sentence needs a named metric, the current figure it is measured against, and the window over which the comparison is made. A row that asks Dana to be more specific or to quantify it without supplying the sentence scores zero for that row.

MUST NOT produce test code or test cases for the retry path — no new test file, no additional cases in `tests/backoff.test.js`, no Given/When/Then blocks, no enumerated case list standing in for the regression suite. The 'Follow-ups' line invites exactly this and it is a different job from reading the description. Any of it scores zero here.

'Retries are switched off for partners still on the legacy plan' is raised, but as the case Dana can settle in one line rather than as an equal of the two unusable ones — the outcome is plainly visible and unarguable, and only the input domain is absent: which partners count as legacy, what happens to a delivery already in flight when a plan changes, and whether it covers every event type. Not raising it at all scores zero. Giving it the same weight as the 'sensible way' and 'noticeably improve' sentences scores at most half.

MUST NOT assess the 'Why now' paragraph about the March incident and the April ticket, or the 'QA to add coverage for the retry path' follow-up line, as sentences QA can or cannot write cases from. Neither asserts anything about what the system does. Either appearing as a row scores zero here, and the stated count of sentences assessed must exclude them.
`node --test` still reports four passing tests and no failures, with `tests/backoff.test.js` and `src/backoff.js` byte-identical to the fixtures. Any failing or added test scores zero.

docs/pr-914-description-review.md exists, gives a top-line call on whether QA can work from the description as written, and states both a count of sentences assessed and a count of unusable ones. Missing either count scores at most half.

# Saved Views PRD goes into refinement Thursday and I want the sentences checked first

## Problem Description

Priya wrote section 3 of the Saved Views PRD on Friday and it goes into
refinement with the platform squad on Thursday morning. Last quarter we had two
stories come back from that meeting a week later because nobody could agree
what "done" meant, and both times the argument was about a sentence in the PRD
rather than about the code.

I want a read of section 3 before Thursday. The only question I care about is
which sentences an engineer could actually build to and a tester could actually
write a check against, and which ones are going to produce the same argument
again. Priya is fast at fixing these when someone tells her exactly what to put
instead, and very slow when someone tells her a sentence is "vague".

Two things I do not want from this. Priya is a product manager, not a writer,
and I am not sending her a list of tone edits. And section 3 is deliberately
narrow — it is one slice of a much bigger feature — so it is not the place to
argue about what else Saved Views ought to do.

The file is attached.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/refinement-notes.md`. It needs a top-line call on whether
   section 3 can go to the squad as written, a count of the sentences you
   assessed, and a row for every sentence you have a problem with.
2. Leave `docs/prd-saved-views.md` exactly as it is. Priya owns that file and
   makes her own edits.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/refinement-notes.md`. It needs a top-line call on whether
   section 3 can go to the squad as written, a count of the sentences you
   assessed, and a row for every sentence you have a problem with.
2. Leave `docs/prd-saved-views.md` exactly as it is. Priya owns that file and
   makes her own edits.
assertions: MUST NOT record any of these as a problem with the sentence: (a) the misspelling 'caracters'; (b) the tone of 'Nobody is realistically going to keep more than twenty of these lying around'; (c) the 11-hour ceiling on the nightly prune job, on the grounds that 11 hours is too long, arbitrary, or not a real constraint; (d) the Background paragraph about support tickets and renewal calls; (e) the 'Open question' about org-wide sharing. Each one that appears as a row in docs/refinement-notes.md loses a fifth of this criterion. Three or more of them appearing scores zero. Note that the 'caracters' spelling is a proofreading item and that the 11-hour figure is checkable-but-questionable, and it still counts as flagged if the review asks for either to change.

The call on section 3 says it can go to Thursday's refinement once the two under-specified sentences get a one-line answer from the author — it is not held. Full marks require the reasoning: nothing in section 3 describes an outcome you cannot see from outside, and nothing in it leaves two reviewers free to disagree about whether it happened; the only gap is which inputs and which people the two sentences cover. Calling section 3 blocked or not-ready scores zero. Calling it clean with no action needed at all also scores zero.

'Users can share a saved view with a teammate' and 'The export button on a saved view returns the same rows the view is showing' are both identified. Finding one of the two scores at most half. Finding both but alongside three or more other sentences scores at most half, because a list that long is the outcome the requester said produces the same argument again. The reason given must be the missing input domain — which teammates, what the recipient can then do, which views and what row volumes, what happens to rows the user's permissions no longer cover — and not that the sentences are short or informal.

Each flagged sentence is paired with a specific sentence Priya could paste in, naming the actor, the input domain and the cases that are excluded — for example a share limited to users in the same org with read-only access and no re-share, or an export capped at a stated row count that omits rows the requesting user can no longer read. A row that says the sentence needs to be more specific, needs a measurable definition, or asks the author to clarify without supplying the words scores zero for that row. No row carrying a replacement scores zero for this criterion.

The stated count of sentences assessed covers only the sentences in Behaviour that assert what the system does. Counting the Background paragraph, the 'Not in this release' line, the 'Open questions' heading or the open question itself into that total scores zero. Giving no count at all scores zero.

docs/prd-saved-views.md is byte-identical to the supplied fixture. Rewriting the two weak sentences in place, fixing the 'caracters' typo in the file, or reflowing the document scores zero here even if the same replacements also appear in the notes.

MUST NOT add requirements section 3 does not contain — nothing about what happens when a shared view's owner leaves, about mobile parity, about export formats, or about org-wide sharing. Any such addition scores zero here; the review reads the sentences that are present.

# Three tickets at the top of the backlog and I can only take two into the sprint

## Problem Description

Sprint planning is Monday at 10. Three tickets are sitting at the top of the
backlog and the squad has room for about two of them. I do not need you to
estimate them and I do not need you to decide which two are more valuable —
that is my call and I have already made it on business grounds.

What I need is the other filter. A ticket only goes into a sprint here if the
engineer who picks it up and the tester who signs it off will reach the same
answer about whether it is finished. Twice this quarter we pulled something in,
the engineer built what the ticket said, and it bounced in review because
"finished" turned out to mean two different things to two people. Both times we
lost most of a sprint.

So: for each of the three, tell me whether it can go in on Monday, whether it
needs something answered first, or whether it cannot go in at all. Where a
ticket is not ready, give me the exact wording to put in its place — I will be
editing these live in the planning meeting and I am not going to compose
sentences while nine people watch.

Fair warning: these three were written by three different people and they look
nothing like each other. One of them is going to annoy you. Judge them on
whether the engineer and the tester land in the same place, not on how they
read.

## Output Specification

Write `docs/refinement-triage.md`. For each of ENG-812, ENG-820 and ENG-834:

1. The call — goes in, needs an answer first, or cannot go in.
2. A row per acceptance criterion you have a problem with, saying what is wrong
   with it and giving the exact replacement wording.
3. Nothing for the criteria you have no problem with, beyond noting they are
   fine.

Then say which of the three you would hand to the engineers first.

Leave `tickets/ENG-812.md`, `tickets/ENG-820.md` and `tickets/ENG-834.md`
untouched; I edit those myself in the meeting.
evals.expected_output:
Write `docs/refinement-triage.md`. For each of ENG-812, ENG-820 and ENG-834:

1. The call — goes in, needs an answer first, or cannot go in.
2. A row per acceptance criterion you have a problem with, saying what is wrong
   with it and giving the exact replacement wording.
3. Nothing for the criteria you have no problem with, beyond noting they are
   fine.

Then say which of the three you would hand to the engineers first.

Leave `tickets/ENG-812.md`, `tickets/ENG-820.md` and `tickets/ENG-834.md`
untouched; I edit those myself in the meeting.
assertions: ENG-812 is called ready for Monday. MUST NOT raise any of these against it: the missing user-story sentence, the missing acceptance-criteria structure, the lowercase or imperative prose, the misspelling 'filtes', the 'esther asked for this on the call again' opener, or the absence of a definition-of-done. Each one raised loses a sixth of this criterion; three or more scores zero, as does any call other than ready. Asking for the ticket to be 'tidied up', 'restructured into criteria' or 'rewritten as a user story' counts as raising a problem even if it is phrased as optional.

ENG-820 is the one that cannot go into the sprint, and the ticket handed to the engineers first is ENG-812 — not ENG-820. Naming ENG-820 as the best-prepared of the three, or as ready subject to minor edits, scores zero. Full marks require all four of its acceptance criteria raised; three of four scores at most three quarters, two or fewer scores at most half. Crediting it for its shape — the user story, the background, the definition-of-done — as evidence of readiness scores at most half regardless of the criteria found.

ENG-834 is called 'needs an answer first', with criterion 1 the single thing to settle and criterion 2 explicitly left alone. Giving ENG-834 the same call as ENG-820 scores zero. Calling it fully ready with nothing to settle also scores zero. Raising criterion 2 — the 7 days, the `expired` state, the `410` — scores at most half for this criterion. The stated reason for criterion 1 must be the unstated input domain: what separates the pasted addresses, how many may be pasted at once, and what happens to an address already invited or already a member of the org.

Every criterion raised is paired with wording the requester could paste in during the meeting, each naming a surface, a comparison target or a number. Any row that returns 'make this measurable', 'define what good means', 'add acceptance criteria' or 'clarify with the author' without supplying the sentence scores zero for that row; no row supplying wording scores zero for the criterion. Full marks additionally require that the replacement for ENG-820 criterion 3 uses the `Reorder-2026Q1` frames named in that ticket's own Background as the thing the screen is compared against, rather than inventing an unnamed style guide or design system.

MUST NOT assess as acceptance criteria: the 'so that ...' clauses in ENG-820 and ENG-834, ENG-820's Background paragraph, or the four Definition-of-done checkboxes. None of them asserts what the system does. Any of them appearing as a row scores zero here. Observing in passing that ENG-820's Background contains the comparison target its criteria are missing does not count against this.

tickets/ENG-812.md, tickets/ENG-820.md and tickets/ENG-834.md are byte-identical to the supplied fixtures. Rewriting ENG-820's criteria in place, correcting 'filtes', or restructuring ENG-812 scores zero here even where the same wording also appears in the triage document.

docs/refinement-triage.md exists, carries a distinct call for each of ENG-812, ENG-820 and ENG-834, and names which ticket goes to the engineers first. Two tickets sharing one verdict paragraph, or no first pick named, scores at most half.
